12: Pescadero Marsh Natural Preserve: Hike the Sequoia Audubon Trail and observe the diverse bird species in the marsh.
13: Coyote Hills Regional Park: Hike the No Name Trail, which winds through marshes and offers glimpses of wildlife.
14: Lake Chabot Regional Park: Follow the West Shore Trail, circling the lake and providing scenic views of the surrounding nature.
15: Las Trampas Regional Wilderness: Hike the Chamise and Mahogany Trails, offering picturesque views of rolling hills and wildflowers.

Follow @outdoorwiseliving for more NorCal discovery!

⚠️ This is an unnamed and unmaintained beach that can be super dangerous.  This is not a recommendation nor is it advice to check out this spot given the unknown integrity of the rope ladder and the threatening surf that can be extremely hazardous with sneaker waves and strong currents.  Exercise the most extreme caution and obey all locally posted signs and warnings.

🅿️: Free, parking at approximately these GPS coordinates: 37.0005429,-122.1801708 on the west side of highway 1.

🥾Trail: From the parking lot, cross the railroad tracks and head north.  You need to be north of Bonny Doon beach and look for the keyhole rock (ie sea cave) about 0.5 miles from the parking lot.  If you see shark fin cove you’ve gone too far (which also has a sea cave but this is different). You’re looking for this location: (36.9970863, -122.1793242)

🏝️: There is a small trail from the top of the bluff (with some soil based stairs) that leads to a ~15 foot drop with a hand ladder assist to access the beach.  The beach is great for finding seaglass, exploring the sea cave (it will be on your left facing the water), and having a private view of the Pacific Ocean.

🛂 Tips: There’s nothing to see when facing the water to the right and sneaker waves can knock you over.  You can place your phone on the back wall to get a great picture.  If you are going to go, time this for low tide to have maximum accessibility for the sea cave.  Bring a change of clothes in case you put your feet in the water.  Now is a great time of year to look for gray whales.

📶 Cell Reception: Yes nearly full

📍Other places to see:  combine this with Shark Fin Cove and Naturals Bridges in Santa Cruz (trail reviews coming soon) if heading South.  Natural bridges has ~7000 monarch butterflies right now.  To the north, combine with the Half Moon Bay area and stop at Pigeon Point Lighthouse in Pescadero

🚮: Always leave no trace.
*****
I’m on a mission to inspire people to spend more time outside by sharing the best Bay Area & beyond places to explore - follow @outdoorwiseliving for more inspiration!

title:
Chicken Tikka Masala Burritos

Frozen Burrito Meal Prep Series,
Episode 2 of 9

Per Burrito (makes 11)
480 Calories
40g Protein
56g Carbs
11g Fat

In this series - I’m going to show you how to bulk prep high protein frozen burritos just like I do. The goal is to make a wide variety of flavor profiles, some familiar burrito flavors and a few fusion flavors, so that you never get bored when meal time rolls around

Every recipe is high protein, low calorie and insanely delicious - the Stealth Health way 🫡

Spice mix:
3 tablespoons smoked paprika
2 tablespoons cumin
1 tablespoon garam masala
1 tablespoon coriander
1 tsp turmeric 
1 tsp cayenne
- Use half in marinade, and half in sauce

Chicken/Marinade:
48oz chicken breast
240g yogurt
2 tablespoons minced garlic
2 tablespoons ginger paste 
Juice of 2 lemons
2 tablespoons salt
1/2 of spice mix

Masala sauce:
30g butter
2 onions, chopped
2 tablespoons minced garlic
2 tablespoons ginger paste 
- Cook onions over high heat until translucent/beginning to brown, add garlic/ginger and sauté for 3-4 minutes

4 tablespoons tomato paste
1/2 of spice mix
- Simmer for 1 min

14.5oz can tomatoes
150ml water
Handful of chopped cilantro/stems
- Simmer for 10-15 minutes, blend until completely smooth

200g low fat Greek yogurt
15g butter
Handful chopped cilantro
Salt to taste
- Add to blended sauce and mix over low simmer 

Grill chicken until charred, about 10 minutes (or bake/broil). It should be slightly undercooked. Dice, add to sauce, cover and simmer for 15-20 minutes

200g basmati rice
350g Chicken bone broth
(I cooked the rice in bone broth for extra protein + flavor, optional)

11 burrito tortillas

Herby Yogurt sauce (for dipping/served w burritos)
600g low fat greek yogurt
Juice of 1 lemon
80ml milk 
15g honey
Chopped Chives/cilantro

Notes/Tips:
- Place meat/rice mixture in a bowl and refrigerate for ~20 minutes. This helps it thicken/makes rolling burritos 100x easier

- Reheat instructions: remove from freezer, wrap in a paper towel, microwave for 2 mins, then air fry at 375 for 6-8 minutes to crisp up your tortilla, or pan fry

I’ve spent 1.5 years in a row in Southeast Asia and this is my perfect itinerary for a calendar year: 

📍Thailand: January- March 
You’ll have the perfect weather all over Thailland. Be careful in the north though, the burning season of the rice fields usually starts somewhere between Febuary and March. Air Quality will be poor during this time. 
A lot of countries will get 60 days for free when entering and you can extend your stay by another 30 days for 50USD. 

📍 Vietnam: April - mid May 
Now is the best time to see the entire country. Vietnam is really long and has different rainy seasons. 
Some countries get 45 days for free or you get the e-visa that’s valid for up to 90 days and it costs 25USD. 

📍 Indonesia: mid May - mid July 
It’s the best time to visit. Dry season just started and it’s before high season kicks in. August seems to be the busiest and most expensive month. 
Get the 30 day e-visa for 30USD and extend it online for another 30days, also for 30USD. 

📍Sri Lanka: mid July - mid September 
This tiny country has different monsoon seasons. The east coast will be in dry season during the time and the famous south in monsoon. I visited the south during July and August 2023 and the weather was beautiful and there was barely any rain. Only downside is that some restaurants are closed. They have shops in the south and in the east and switch between seasons. 
Get the 60 day  e-visa for 75USD. 

📍Vietnam: mid September- mid October 
Now it’s time to visit northern Vietnam for all the stunning rice fields. 

📍Thailand: mid October- November 
Visit northern Thailand during this time and you’ll get the most beautiful landscapes. Everything is lush and green. 

📍Laos/Cambodia/Thailand: December 
All countries have perfect weather, Thailand might get expensive around Christmas and new years. 
I loooved Laos and can highly recommend it. 
Get the 30 day visa on arrival for 40USD. I heard it’s super easy to extend.

HAVE YOU HAD AUTHENTIC YAKITORI?🍢😋
•
🔖 Bookmark this legendary Tokyo restaurant that’s now in SF Japantown! 
•
📍 Yakitori Edomasa - San Francisco, CA 
•
Chicken skewers and beer are one of my favorite foodie combos and I’m so happy we now have an authentic yakitori restaurant in @sf_japantown ! Straight from Tokyo, Japan comes the legendary @yakitori_edomasa_official ! Each skewer is grilled to tender, juicy perfection and their menu invites you to try other parts of the chicken you wouldn’t normally see, but are SO flavorful! 
•
Kissed by the flames of a charcoal grill, their yakitori is made to order so every stick comes out piping hot and has lovely smoky notes. I tried their $30 Edomasa tasting menu and got a full taste of the many chicken dishes they have to offer!
•
We started with the Chicken Paitan soup and their hearty tataki meatball. The broth was ultra rich and so soothing with every sip. Then you get to indulge in their many skewers with cuts ranging from juicy chicken breast with grilled scallion to crispy skin and chicken heart! 
•
My favorite skewer was actually one of their add-on’s — the sasami or chicken tender with wasabi. I would have never thought to put wasabi on chicken, but this is a combo I did not know I needed! The meat is lightly brushed with a sweet and umami yakitori sauce, then topped with small dollops of wasabi. This added such a nice bite to the meat and cuts the sweetness beautifully. Their wasabi alone was so good! Highly recommend trying this in addition to the Edomasa! 
•
If you love chicken skewers or are looking to try some authentic Japanese yakitori, you need to check out this latest addition to Japantown! Thank you so much @yakitori_edomasa_official for having me!🫶🏼

Meet a 34 year old married couple earning $175,000 after taxes—and they’ve added an incredible wealth-building tool: a short-term rental (STR) property!

They live in a modest home w/ a mortgage locked in at subpar 3% rates. 

Here’s how they’re securing financial freedom for their family:

1️⃣ Income from Their STR Property

Net $3,000/month ($36,000/year) from their rental property—above and beyond his income.

Tax benefits they enjoy:
• Depreciation deductions to lower taxable income
• Write-offs on property expenses (maintenance, utilities, etc.)
• Travel expense deductions when visiting the property for management purposes
• Offset taxes with any passive losses

$90,000 in emergency savings in a HYSA
They contribute $10,000 annually to build more security

title:
Invisible Apple Cake ✨🍎 (Gâteau Invisible Aux Pommes) Recipe below 👇

Edit: lots of questions about the cut proof gloves! If you comment ‘link’, I’ll send you the ones we use + our mandoline. 

This beautiful French dessert is made by layering a TON of thinly sliced apples in a custard-like batter. The apples almost disappear into the cake, hence the name! 

It’s somewhat similar to clafoutis, but with a much higher ratio of fruit to batter. This cake is also not too sweet, and it’s made almost entirely with fresh apples! 

You can serve it with anything from powdered sugar, to whipped cream, to ice cream and/or caramel sauce. We used our apple cider syrup for topping (you can find the recipe a few posts back). 

Bookmark the RECIPE below 👇 and don’t forget to follow @crowded_kitchen for more easy, seasonal recipes! 

INVISIBLE APPLE CAKE

1 cup all purpose flour 
1 tsp baking powder 
1/2 tsp cinnamon 
1/4 tsp nutmeg 
1/4 tsp ginger 
Pinch of cloves
1/4 tsp salt
2 tbsp melted butter (unsalted)
1/2 cup whole milk (room temp)
1 tsp vanilla extract (or vanilla bean paste)
3 large eggs 
2/3 cup granulated sugar 
2 lb apples, peeled and sliced 1/8-inch thick 

Preheat oven to 375˚F. Grease and line a loaf pan with parchment paper. 

Using a knife or a mandoline, slice apples into 1/8” slices. 

In a bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder and spices. 

In a separate small bowl, whisk together melted butter, milk and vanilla. 

In a separate large bowl, beat eggs and sugar for 90 seconds on medium speed, until pale. Add half of the flour mixture and mix on low speed until combined, then add the butter/milk mixture, then the remaining flour, mixing just until the batter comes together.

Add the apples to the bowl and gently toss until they are evenly coated in the batter. 

Layer the apples into the prepared loaf pan. Pour any remaining batter in the pan. Bake for ~75 minutes until golden brown around the edges and a toothpick comes out clean. It may take longer depending on how thick your apple slices are.  Let cool for at least one hour before slicing and serving.

1. Your Weekly Wins Archive

Every Friday, write down one win from the week. A project you shipped, a skill you learned, a conversation that mattered. By December, you’ll have 52 proof points for your next promotion or job search.

2. LinkedIn Thought Library

Once a week, save one industry insight, lesson learned, or observation about your work. Not polished posts. Just raw notes. By Q4, you’ll have a year’s worth of content ideas and a clear POV in your field.

3. The Monthly Mentor Coffee

Once a month, reach out to someone whose career you admire. Ask one thoughtful question. 12 conversations = a network that actually opens doors and a clearer picture of where you’re headed.

4. The Industry Pulse Tracker

Pick 5 leaders or publications in your field. Spend 15 minutes every Sunday seeing what they’re talking about. By December, you’ll spot trends before your peers and have informed opinions that make you stand out.

January through December, ship something every 30 days. A side project, a new process at work, a presentation, a piece of content. 12 months = 12 tangible proof points that you execute, not just plan.

Send one cold email or DM every week to someone you want to learn from or work with. No asks, just value or genuine curiosity. 52 messages = opportunities you never would’ve had by waiting to be discovered.

Every week, share something publicly. A LinkedIn post, a project update, a lesson learned, a portfolio piece. 52 posts = visibility, credibility, and inbound opportunities you can’t get by staying quiet.

8. The Monthly Skill Sprint

Pick one skill gap that’s holding you back. Spend 30 days closing it by taking a course, building a project, practicing daily. 12 months = 12 new capabilities that completely change what you’re qualified for.

The stalder handstand press-up is built on the ability to compress your legs tightly against your chest while maintaining a strong push through your arms and opening your shoulders to align with your body. Strengthening these actions through targeted exercises will bring you closer to achieving a successful a handstand stalder press-up.

There are many exercises that can help build strength in these positions, but it’s difficult to fully isolate each action independently. In this exercise, however, the focus is on compression. By maximizing your push through the floor to elevate your body and using the wall to keep your legs as high as possible, you achieve an enhanced level of compression that would be hard to replicate by simply pushing yourself into an L-sit from the floor.

As you perform this handstand  stalder press-up exercise, you’ll notice how much you can actually compress. You’re essentially carving a pathway in your body to reach maximum compression, building the strength needed to maintain it. This way, when you initiate the press-up, your starting position will feature a deeper compression, allowing you to keep your legs as close to your body as possible. From there, you can focus on opening the shoulders to transition smoothly into a handstand.

How to perform the exercise:

Start with your feet against the wall, legs bent, and your hands positioned at hip height.
Rock your body towards the wall, pushing yourself as high as possible off the ground.
Once elevated, stretch your legs while keeping your back rounded over yourself. Your hips should pass over your arms, and you want to keep them as high as possible.
Hold this position for about 5 seconds before slowly rocking back towards the wall and repeating.
You can perform 3 to 5 repetitions per set, aiming for 3 sets in total.

1. Japanese Trains:
Eating and drinking on trains in Japan is generally not acceptable. The only time where eating and drinking on the train is ok is on regional long-distance trains, like Shinkansen, where every seat has a tray and cup holder.
Many people use their cell phones while on the train. However, be sure that your phone use does not disturb others. Never talk on your phone while on the train, unless using the designated phone area of the Shinkansen.
While you may be accustomed to chatting with your traveling companions while using public transportation, this is not the norm in Japan. Loud chatter or other disturbance is considered rude. You may notice that most Japanese train passengers stand or sit in silence.
2. Escalator Etiquette:
People stand on the left side of the escalator in the East side of Japan including Tokyo leaving the space on the right for the walking traffic. It’s the opposite on the West side of Japan, especially Osaka.
3. Tipping:
Do not try to tip in Japan. Tipping is not customary and can even be considered rude or insulting. The Japanese culture places a high emphasis on service and hospitality so good service is considered a standard. Simple “Arigato” - “Thank you” can be enough to show your gratitude.
4. Chopsticks:
Do not place your chopsticks vertically in your dish.
If you want to give a friend a bite of your food to try, place it on a plate or bowl instead of transferring it from your chopsticks to theirs.
Rubbing your chopsticks to remove splinters is considered rude.
Lay your chopsticks on the table instead of across your dish.
Don’t stab your food with chopsticks.
5. Walking while eating is considered rude in Japan:
It implies that the person isn’t taking the time to appreciate their meal properly or respect those who prepared it for them, which goes against traditional values. Additionally, walking while eating can create messes on public streets which can be seen as disrespectful. So even if you are buying from the street vendors, after receiving your food, find a spot next to the food stand to enjoy and finish your meal before you continue walking.
.
Safe travels friends ❤️
.

Kioi-Seido was designed by architect Hiroshi Naito and opened in 2021. 

It stands out in the neighbourhood as a 15-meter tall, four-story concrete cube without windows, enveloped by a glass facade and supported by four columns. 

What sets this structure apart is that the RINRI Institute of Ethics, the client, provided no specific purpose for the building. Instead, the usage was meant to adapt to the completed construction. 

Hiroshi Naito embraced this challenge, creating a building without a predefined function. Kioi-Seido is envisioned to be open to projects of all kinds, symbolized by its ground floor with four columns serving as an open, inviting gallery space. From the outside, a staircase leads into the “cube,” consisting of four light-filled floors connected by an elegant staircase.
